posts.title: Early Action vs Early Decision: Which One Should You Choose?

Applying to college can feel like stepping into a maze. Deadlines, essays, recommendations—it's easy to get overwhelmed. Then there's the choice between Early Action (EA) and Early Decision (ED), and suddenly one more decision feels like it could change everything. But understanding the difference isn't just about deadlines—it's about strategy, priorities, and sometimes, risk.

What is Early Action?

Early Action is like raising your hand first in class: you show interest, but you're not committing to anything yet. You simply apply early and get your decision back by December. Easy! If you're accepted, you can celebrate a little victory while still weighing your other options.

EA gives you the space to compare schools, scholarships, and financial aid packages before you commit in May. It's an approach that balances ambition with caution. You're signaling to colleges that you're serious... but you're not trapped into a single choice. In short, EA is early, but not binding.

Pros of Early Action:

  • You get decisions early, reducing senior-year stress.
  • You retain the flexibility to compare multiple schools and financial aid packages.
  • Shows colleges that you are proactive and serious.
  • Less pressure—no binding commitment.

Cons of Early Action:

  • You must have your application polished by fall.
  • Some schools offer Restrictive or Single-Choice Early Action, limiting where else you can apply early.
  • Early submission may feel rushed for students who want more time to improve their application.

What is Early Decision?

Early Decision, on the other hand, is a full commitment. Apply ED, and if you're accepted, you're going. No ifs, no maybes. Deadlines are similar to EA, but the stakes are higher.

ED often comes with slightly better odds at selective schools (because admissions officers know you're fully invested), but it also comes with serious responsibility. You can't compare financial aid packages. You can't back out for another opportunity. You're choosing certainty over flexibility.

It's a strategic gamble: a potential shortcut to your dream school, but one that demands confidence and preparation.

Pros of Early Decision:

  • Higher chances of acceptance at many selective schools due to demonstrated commitment.
  • Reduces stress later—you know your college plans early.
  • Shows admissions officers you have a clear top choice, which can strengthen your application.

Cons of Early Decision:

  • Binding commitment—if admitted, you must attend.
  • No ability to compare financial aid packages or scholarship offers.
  • Risky if you're still uncertain about your top choice or need more time to strengthen your application.

How to Decide?

  • Early Action is right if...
    You want early results without committing. Maybe you're still comparing schools, uncertain about costs, or hoping for multiple options. EA gives you breathing room while keeping the advantage of applying early.
  • Early Decision is right if...
    You have a clear #1 school, you're confident in your application, and you're comfortable committing before knowing financial aid packages. ED is a path for those ready to take a calculated risk for potentially higher acceptance odds.

Think of it this way: EA is an early handshake. ED is a signed contract. Both get your name in front of admissions officers sooner, but one keeps the door open, while the other locks it.

Ending Thoughts

The choice between Early Action and Early Decision isn't just about timing—it's about knowing yourself, your goals, and your financial situation. If you want flexibility and want to keep doors open, EA is your friend. If you're certain about your dream school and willing to commit, ED could give you that extra edge.

At the end of the day, the "right" choice is the one that reduces stress and keeps you confident in your path forward. Remember, no single deadline defines your future; your persistence, growth, and authenticity matter most.

What is the UC System?

When it comes to applying to college in California, few systems are as well-known (or as competitive )as the University of California (UC) system. With nine undergraduate campuses stretching from all across California, the UC system offers world-class academics, vibrant campus communities, and a commitment to public service and research. But for many students and families, understanding how the UC system works can feel overwhelming.

The 9 UC Campuses locations

Here’s a quick snapshot of the undergraduate UC campuses:

  1. UC Berkeley – Northern California, San Francisco Bay Area
  2. UCLA – Los Angeles, Westwood neighborhood
  3. UC San Diego – Southern California, La Jolla (San Diego)
  4. UC Santa Barbara – Central Coast, beachside city of Santa Barbara
  5. UC Irvine – Southern California, Orange County
  6. UC Davis – Northern California, just west of Sacramento
  7. UC Santa Cruz – Coastal Northern California, redwood forests near Monterey Bay
  8. UC Riverside – Inland Southern California, part of the Inland Empire
  9. UC Merced – Central Valley, newest and fastest-growing UC campus

Each campus has its own culture, strengths, and areas of specialization—from Berkeley’s research legacy to Santa Barbara’s oceanfront labs. Whether you’re interested in engineering, liberal arts, sustainability, or pre-med, there’s likely a UC that fits your goals. And below is a little more information of the schools in Comparison by the numbers

By the numbers

Rankings

While rankings are just one factor to consider, they often play a large role in shaping public perception and student interest. Within the University of California system, UC Berkeley and UCLA consistently stand out with both frequently ranking among the top 15 universities globally. Berkeley is renowned for its excellence in engineering, computer science, and the social sciences, while UCLA is highly regarded for its strong programs in the life sciences, film, and business.

Below these Universities in the UC System would be: UC San Diego (UCSD), UC Santa Barbara (UCSB), UC Irvine (UCI), and UC Davis. These four schools are highly respected and offer strong academics, but are slightly less selective than Tier 1.

Then below these schools would be UC Santa Cruz, Riverside, and Merced. These campuses are less selective but still provide an excellent education with access to UC resources.

With all this in mind, Rankings should never be the only metric in deciding where to apply, but they can help students understand each UC’s academic strengths and global reputation. More importantly, finding the right fit—academically, socially, and financially—matters far more than a number on a list.

Application Process

Applying to the University of California system is a unique experience as it has its own application platform, deadlines, and requirements. The good news? You only need to fill out one application to apply to any or all of the nine UC undergraduate campuses.

Here’s a breakdown of the key steps:

  1. Create a UC Application Account
  2. Pick Your Campuses
  3. Input Academic History
  4. Answer 4 out of 8 Personal Insight Questions (PIQs)
  5. List your Activities & Awards
  6. Application Fees & Waivers ($80 per)
  7. Review & Submit by November 30

Tuition & Cost

The University of California is a public state university system, which means it’s primarily funded to serve California residents. As such, tuition is significantly lower for in-state students.

  • California Residents: $14,436 per year
  • Non-Residents: $14,436 + $34,200 in non-resident supplemental tuition (Totaling over $48,000 annually)

Because of their prestige and global recognition, UC campuses receive tens of thousands of applications from students across the U.S. and around the world each year. To balance this demand with their public mission, the UC system charges an additional non-resident tuition fee to out-of-state and international students. This helps ensure that California taxpayer funding continues to prioritize access for in-state students while still welcoming talented applicants from beyond the state.

A Brief Overview

Here’s a quick snapshot:

  • UC Berkeley – Known for computer science, engineering, economics, and political science. A historic campus with a strong activist and research culture.
  • UCLA – Strong in pre-med, psychology, film & television, and business. Located in Los Angeles with a competitive but energetic vibe.
  • UC San Diego – A leader in biology, neuroscience, engineering, and oceanography. Offers a unique college system and coastal campus.
  • UC Davis – Top-ranked in animal science, environmental science, agriculture, and biological sciences. Known for a bike-friendly, community-centered campus.
  • UC Irvine – Rising in reputation with standout programs in computer science, public health, and business. Located in Orange County with a modern, STEM-forward feel.
  • UC Santa Barbara – Offers strong programs in physics, environmental studies, and marine biology. Known for its beachside location and balanced social-academic scene.
  • UC Santa Cruz – Recognized for computer science, astrophysics, and environmental science. A forested, progressive campus with a laid-back culture.
  • UC Riverside – Strong in entomology, business, and STEM fields. A diverse and supportive campus focused on upward mobility.
  • UC Merced – The newest UC, growing quickly with strengths in engineering, environmental systems, and public health. Known for small class sizes and innovation.

Each campus has its own flavor, opportunities, and strengths—and what’s best for one student might not be right for another.

👉 Want to learn more? In our other blog post, we’ll break down each UC in detail to help you find your best match.

Welcome to Aggie Life

The letter has arrived, and you have been accepted into UC Davis. Unsure of what awaits you on campus, you may picture what everyone says about it: Cows, biking, friendly students, and more cows. These are all true in fact! (maybe not as much about the cows) but there is much more to aggie life than this.

Davis at a glance

UC Davis is located in a small town west of Sacramento where the population is students, staff, and young families. Davis is through and through a college town, as the town is almost 100% based around the college. The town has 3 parts: the school, downtown and housing for students. The school bleeds right into downtown so the borders between campus and town are hardly there.

Davis due to its large number of International students, has a high number of asian restaurants, shops, grocery stores, and boba. There are probably more boba places in Davis than maybe all of the rest of the surrounding towns combined. This is far outside of the normal concentration for Asian culture in the central valley and by comparison is like an oasis in a desert.

The downtown is small, quaint and very aesthetic. It has a very charming farmers market every Wednesday and Saturday and is very walkable from end to end. The main street that many students frequent is G street with its two rivaling coffee shops (Temple and Pachamama) and many bars and restaurants.

Outside of downtown in the residential areas, all of the places (outside of far east Davis and far south Davis) feel very connected to the centre and school due to the excellent UC Davis free bus transport system.

Student Life on Campus

Despite UC Davis being the largest of all the UC Campus’s, there are 2 main areas of action on campus. One would be the MU and the other being the Silo.

The MU is the heart of student life at Davis. It is the central hub where most bus lines stop so many students are passing in and out of this region. There are ample places to grab food, study, and hang out between classes. Inside, the MU has the UC Davis Bookstore, Amazon lockers, a bowling alley/pool and gaming area (All it doesn't have is good food or coffee). The Freeborn Hall and Coffee House (aka the CoHo) are especially popular, although not very good -but this is just my opinion!

On the other side of campus is the Silo. This hotspot (also due to bus lines being routed to this as the stopping point) is the food trucks and food haven. It has a Peets coffee, lots of eateries, tons of outdoor and indoor settings and proximity to several lecture halls. During lunch hours, it's one of the liveliest places on campus, with students crowding picnic tables or relaxing on the grass between classes. The Silo also houses bike services and student job opportunities, making it a practical stop as much as a social one.

If not in these two areas, there are many halls and lots of campus to explore. From the beautiful lake and arboretum to the odd bathroom in an unnamed hall with a bed in it, there is much to see.

Student life off campus

Between studying and having fun with friends you might forget you need to sleep, or where to sleep; well have no fear as this section will solve those issues. UC Davis provides one-year guaranteed housing for eligible first-year freshmen, with meal plans included and options to join Living-Learning Communities (LLCs) based on interests and identities So yippee! Over 90% of freshmen live in the Residents hall so it isn't required but you would definitely miss out on meeting lots of potential friends.

For freshmen there are 3 dorm options:

  1. Segundo – Northwest Traditional, doubles/triples; central location
  2. Tercero – Southwest, Triples; near STEM buildings
  3. Cuarto – Just northwest of central campus (basically off campus)

The best by location would probably be Tercero but it is the oldest so ehhh not the best. Segundo would probably be the best one as Cuarto is the newest, bigger rooms, and the best food but it is pretty far off campus so walking to classes would not be an option. But if the pros outweigh the main cons the Cuarto is for you!

For Sophomore, Transfers, and all other grade levels you have 4 options

  1. The Green at West Village - University Run “on campus housing”
  2. Sol at West Village - University Run “on campus housing”
  3. Orchard Park - University Run “on campus housing”
  4. Off Campus living - all on you

So a common option for the sophomore students and transfers who don't know better options go with the Green at West village. So the Green is a very interesting place, imagine a soviet era apartment block on the outside and plasticy hotel apartment interiors - sound good to you? They are not the worst but certainly not the best option. Rooms come in singles, doubles, and quads each and you have to pick them based on a competitive time slot lottery. The students don't tend to be social here and stay to themselves and only communicate through the discord.

Sol at West village is in the same area as the green but it is slightly better but this housing is oddly very popular with international students. There are many different housing layouts and some of the unlikely souls get their apartments on the ground floor right in front of the bus stop, truly a fate worse than death. But unlike the green, students tend to be social and there is a pool so that is a great plus!

Orchard park is a newer apartment complex which was designed for grad students. It is similar in look and design to the Green but the rooms are nicer and slightly bigger for better value. You most likely wont do this unless you are a 5th year senior or grad student so do not be concerned with this option.

Lastly would be off campus housing, the potential best or worst option depending on where you live. Housing is really quite competitive so it is best to know who you are living with and find a place in January/February and sign a lease in February/March for the best pick of apartments. There are many options and ranges of pricing, it is best to ask juniors and seniors in your clubs to see what they would recommend living in.

Pros and Cons

Below is some pros and cons broken down into a more manageable viewing:

Pros:

  • Bike-Friendly Culture: Davis is one of the most bike-friendly campuses in the nation, making it easy and cheap to get around.
  • Tight-Knit Community: The small college-town feel means you’ll constantly run into friends and have a strong sense of belonging.
  • Strong Academics & Research Opportunities: Especially in STEM, agriculture, and veterinary sciences.
  • International & Diverse: The town has a surprisingly global culture for its size, reflected in food, clubs, and student demographics.
  • Beautiful Outdoors: Arboretum, farmers market, and proximity to NorCal destinations (Sacramento, SF, Lake Tahoe).

Cons:

  • Small-Town Limits: Davis can feel slow or “sleepy,” especially compared to bigger UC cities like LA or Berkeley.
  • Housing Competition: Off-campus housing is competitive and can get expensive relative to the town’s size.
  • Weather: Summers are very hot, and winters can be rainy and foggy.
  • Limited Nightlife: Bars and social life exist, but options are minimal; you’ll likely need to head to Sacramento for more variety.
  • Food Quality on Campus: Many students complain the dining commons and CoHo aren’t great; most prefer off-campus dining.

Food, Coffee, and more: Where to eat and hang out

Coffee & Study Spots:

  • Temple Coffee – good coffee but expensive, always packed with students but limited outlets for computers.
  • Pachamama – Right across from Temple; more relaxed vibes and often less crowded. Limited seating but excellent seasonal coffee drinks
  • Mishka’s Café – Classic Davis coffee shop with cozy seating and late hours; perfect for midterms and finals season. Decent number of outlets and seating but the coffee isn't as good as the two above.
  • Cloud Forest Café – A little farther from downtown, but quiet and some think it is underrated. Some decent seating and a good number of outlets

Boba:

With the absurd boba density, some are lacking but other are great:

  • Teaspoon – expensive but excellent quality.
  • Lazi Cow – Instagram-famous for its giant drinks and funky decor.
  • Sharetea – Classic chain, solid milk tea.

Food Favorites:

There are many places to eat and if you want to try everything go ahead, but these are the best and you can skip the rest.

  • Taqueria Guadalajara – One of the best spots for cheap and filling Mexican food.
  • The Davis Farmers Market – Wednesdays and Saturdays.
  • Sophia’s Thai Kitchen – Great Thai food and a fun rooftop bar vibe in summer.
  • Yakitori Shoukudo – Great Japanese food and excellent ramen.

Senior year flies by. For high school seniors, September is the best time to get ahead on college applications and scholarships. By tackling these 5 essential tasks now, you'll reduce stress, stay organized, and put yourself in the best position for admissions success.

1. Finalize your college list: know where you want to go

Now, yes right, is the time to finalize your college list. A strong, balanced list sets the foundation for a smooth application season. By early fall:

  • Confirm each school's application deadlines (early action, early decision, and regular decision).
  • Review admission requirements like test policies, supplemental essays, and portfolio submissions.
  • Ensure your list fits your academic profile, financial needs, and personal goals.
  • Make sure your college list is balanced between reaches, target schools and safeties.

2. Start Drafting Your Personal Statement and Essays

Your essays are your biggest and best chance to stand out. Starting early is key as stress is the biggest factor in a poor essay. Every word counts so give yourself extra time so early this September:

  • Brainstorm personal stories that give a window into who you are and why those stories matter to you.
  • Review prompts for the Common App, UC PIQs, or other school-specific essays.
  • Ask your college counselor, or school teacher for early feedback so you can revise before deadlines.

3. Request Letters of Recommendation Early

Your teachers and counselors may soon be overwhelmed with letter of recommendation requests. On top of their everyday work tasks, this season can be extremely busy so a letter of recommendation is a lot to add to their plate. Ask a few weeks after school has started to give them some time and ask in person if you can! To help them help you:

  • Choose recommenders who know you well academically and personally. Make sure at least one is from a core class (Math, English, Science, History)
  • Provide a brag sheet or resume with activities, leadership, and achievements.
  • Remind them of a moment in class where you displayed strong character, or how their teaching impacted you in the classroom and outside.
  • Be patient with them, don't send follow up emails everyday and remind them if there are no updates 2 weeks before the deadline.
  • Confirm submission methods (Common App, UC portal, etc.) and deadlines with your letter of recommendation writer.

4. Organize your application timeline

Senior year is full of fun activities, from senior sunrises, to sports games and trying to do everything you wanted to in High school, deadlines will sneak up fast. Start in September being focused by building a simple tracking system:

  • Use a spreadsheet or planner to list application due dates, essay requirements, and testing info.
  • Break tasks into steps: draft essays, edit, request transcripts, and submit.
  • Aim to finish applications at least a week before each official deadline.

5. Research Scholarships and Financial Aid

A mistake that I often see is students wait until winter to start thinking about financial aid. It is key for students to start early in fall to take time to see what scholarships suit them best and what are the requirements and deadlines for each.

  • Search for national, local, and school-specific scholarships. Use Fastwebb, Big futures, and Niche for the best scholarship search engines.
  • Gather tax and income documents to prepare for the FAFSA and CSS Profile. Give your parents time to find the information.
  • Ask your school counselor about community-based awards not widely advertised, and what scholarships the school offers for students.

Bottom line: September is your chance to take control of your college journey. Start early, stay organized, and you'll thank yourself when deadlines roll around. Need more help with applications or scholarships? Contact me or follow on facebook or Instagram for more college admissions tips!

What is SAT and What is the ACT?

Before the 1900s, many colleges relied on their own aptitude or intelligence tests to decide who was eligible for admission. There was no standardization. Each university had its own exam making the process confusing and inconsistent for students.

To address this, a group of prestigious institutions—including Columbia, Cornell, and Harvard—came together to form the College Entrance Examination Board, a nonprofit organization with the goal of centralizing and standardizing the admissions testing process.

The SAT (Scholastic Aptitude Test) eventually emerged from this effort, designed to measure students’ reasoning and problem-solving abilities. But not everyone agreed with this approach.

In 1960, a professor in Iowa introduced the ACT (American College Testing) as an alternative. Unlike the SAT, the ACT focused more on curriculum-based learning—in other words, it tested what students were actually being taught in school, rather than abstract reasoning.

Today, both the SAT and ACT are accepted by most U.S. colleges—but they have different formats, scoring systems, and skill focuses. (More on that in the next section!)

This is the breakdown of the ACT!

The ACT:

So here we begin with the ever popular in the midwest and east coast is the ACT. The ACT is an achievement-based college admissions exam that focuses on what students have actually learned in school. If you like a straightforward assignment then the ACT’s is right for you. And if you work better under time pressure and are more STEM focused than these are another few reasons to like the ACT.

Test Format and Timing

The ACT consists of 215 multiple-choice questions divided into four main sections where each section only accounts for 25% of your score:

  • English
  • Math
  • Reading
  • Science

The full test takes around 3 hours and 30 minutes to complete (including a short but needed break). The Actual testing time (not including breaks) is 2 hours and 55 minutes

There’s also an optional writing section (essay), which adds an additional 40 minutes if selected. Some colleges require it, but many do not.

The is quite simple Scoring:

  • Each section is scored on a scale of 1 to 36
  • Your composite score is the average of your four section scores, also on a 1–36 scale
  • The optional writing section is scored separately

The SAT:

Now here we go into the popular West Coast college gatekeeper in the SAT. The SAT is a reasoning-based college admissions exam, originally designed to measure how well you can think critically and apply knowledge in unfamiliar ways. If you're someone who prefers logic puzzles, pattern recognition, and slightly more time per question, the SAT might feel like a better fit!

Test Format and Timing

The SAT is now adaptive, meaning the test adjusts its difficulty based on how you perform during the first section of each subject. It’s divided into two main sections:

  • Reading & Writing
  • Math

Each section is split into two modules. You’ll answer easier questions in the first module, and based on your performance, the second module will become more or less challenging.

The full testing time is just under 2 hours and 15 minutes!

Scoring

  • Each section is scored on a scale of 200 to 800
  • Your total SAT score is the sum of both sections, with a maximum score of 1600
  • There’s no essay section on the SAT

The SAT leans slightly more toward reading comprehension and logical reasoning, especially in its math and verbal sections. There’s also less time pressure per question compared to the ACT, which some students find helpful.

But truly the only reason why someone would prefer the SAT is the ample amount of Free testing resources.

Study Resources:

So as mentioned above, the SAT I think has much better study materials than the ACT by a pretty decent margin. But this is when it comes to free resources, so if you plan to pay then they are about equal.

The SAT stands out largely because of its partnership with Khan Academy. It has free, personalized study plans based on your PSAT or SAT scores, Full-length practice tests, Step-by-step math tutorials Reading and writing drills modeled directly after SAT questions. So it is quite useful! There are also tons of youtube videos and free Practice tests online. The SAT test partner Bluebook also has free, self-guided test preparation questions and full-length practice exams.

The ACT on the other hand has limited free resources that lack depth. The platform includes: One free full-length practice test, A few subject-specific question sets, and basic study tips and general advice.

Now when It comes to paid resources the best study books I recommend are the SAT or ACT study panda book and for online resources the Kaplan SAT or ACT prep is great.

If you want to do the 100% free route then the SAT is the right test for you.

Testing Day:

The day has arrived! Make sure you have everything ready: your printed admission ticket, a valid photo ID, two No. 2 pencils, an approved calculator, and some snacks and water for the break. Wear comfortable clothes and set an early alarm to avoid rushing.

Arrive at your testing center early—doors typically close around 8:00 a.m., and late arrivals aren’t allowed to test. Once seated, listen carefully to instructions and stay calm. You've put in the work, and now it's just about pacing yourself. The SAT allows a bit more time per question, while the ACT moves faster, especially in the reading and science sections. If a question stumps you, move on and come back later if there’s time.

During the break, step outside if allowed, eat a quick snack, and hydrate. Once you’re done, take a breath. SAT scores usually come out in two to three weeks, and ACT scores in about ten to fourteen days. Review your results when they’re released and decide whether to send them, retake the test, or move forward with your applications.

Understanding Stanford's Selectivity

Stanford University remains one of the most prestigious and selective institutions in the United States. It combines rigorous academics, a stunning Silicon Valley campus, elite Division I athletics, and a network of distinguished alumni—spanning tech founders like the creators of Google and Instagram, Supreme Court Justices, astronauts, Pulitzer Prize-winning authors, groundbreaking inventors, and even a U.S. President.

But with that prestige comes intense competition. Stanford's acceptance rate hovers around 3.6–3.9%, making it one of the hardest universities in the world to get into. With tens of thousands of applicants competing for roughly 1,700 spots, understanding what Stanford values is crucial to crafting a competitive application.

If Stanford is your dream school, here's what current data reveals about Stanford admission requirements, what the admissions committee prioritizes, and specific strategies to maximize your chances of acceptance.

Academic Profile of Recent Stanford Admits

To understand what you're competing against, here's the academic profile of recently admitted students:

GPA Requirements

  • Average GPA: ~3.95 (unweighted)
  • About 94% of admits earned a 3.75 or higher
  • Nearly 96% graduated in the top 10% of their high school class

SAT and ACT Scores

  • SAT Middle 50%: 1500-1570
  • ACT Middle 50%: 33-35

Rigorous Coursework

  • Most admitted students completed 8-12+ Advanced Placement (AP), International Baccalaureate (IB), or dual-enrollment courses
  • Demonstrates ability to handle college-level work

Important 2025 Update

Stanford will reinstate the required SAT/ACT submission starting with the Fall 2026 application cycle. Students applying for the Class of 2029 and beyond should plan to submit strong standardized test scores. For more details, visit Stanford's official admissions website.

What Does Stanford University Look For?

Since nearly all Stanford applicants are academically excellent, the admissions committee looks deeper than just grades and scores. According to Stanford's Common Data Set, here are the factors considered in application review:

Very Important Factors:

  • Rigor of secondary school coursework
  • Class rank
  • Grade point average (GPA)
  • Standardized test scores (returning as mandatory)
  • Application essays
  • Teacher and counselor recommendations

Important Factors:

  • Extracurricular activities
  • Talent and ability
  • Character and personal qualities

Considered:

  • Alumni/ae relation (though California banned legacy admissions beginning in 2025)
  • First-generation college student status
  • Interviews (when available)
  • Volunteer work and community service
  • Work experience

Not Considered:

  • State residency
  • Religious affiliation
  • Level of applicant's interest

The Four Pillars of a Strong Stanford Application

1. Academic Excellence

Your grades, test scores, and course selection form the foundation of your Stanford application. Stanford seeks students who are intellectually prepared to thrive in one of the nation's most rigorous academic environments.

Action Steps:

  • Target a 3.9+ unweighted GPA throughout high school
  • Aim for a 1540+ SAT or 34+ ACT to be competitive
  • Enroll in the most challenging courses available at your school—honors, AP, IB, or dual enrollment
  • Demonstrate consistent academic performance across all subject areas

Selective colleges like Stanford use tools like the Academic Index (a formula combining GPA and test scores) to initially filter applicants. Strong academics keep you in consideration, but they won't guarantee admission on their own.

2. Intellectual Curiosity

Stanford students are defined by their genuine love of learning and innovation. The admissions committee looks for applicants who pursue knowledge and ideas beyond classroom requirements—students who ask "why" and "what if?"

Ways to Demonstrate Intellectual Curiosity:

  • Conduct independent research in areas that fascinate you
  • Lead or actively participate in academic clubs, competitions, or olympiads
  • Secure internships or mentorships with professors, researchers, or industry professionals
  • Launch independent projects that explore questions you care about
  • Start community initiatives that apply your learning to real-world problems
  • Take online courses or attend summer programs in subjects that excite you

Ask yourself: "How do I spend my free time in ways that energize and fulfill me intellectually?"

3. Authentic Impact

Stanford seeks future leaders and changemakers who use their skills, character, and passion to make a meaningful difference in their communities and beyond. Admissions officers strongly prefer depth over breadth...

Examples of Authentic Impact:

  • Founding a nonprofit or social initiative that addresses a genuine need
  • Leading teams in sports, performing arts, debate, STEM competitions, or student government
  • Sustained volunteering in areas connected to your personal values and experiences
  • Collaborating with others to solve real problems in creative ways
  • Creating measurable change through your efforts—lives touched, funds raised, awareness generated

Admissions officers strongly prefer depth over breadth. A few long-term commitments showing leadership, growth, and genuine impact will always outweigh a scattered resume of superficial activities joined for college applications.

4. Compelling Essays

Stanford's supplemental essays are famously personal, open-ended, and critical to your application success. Your essays provide the opportunity to connect your academic achievements and extracurricular record to your values, personal journey, and future potential.

Stanford's Required Essays Typically Include:

  • An idea, experience, or topic that excites your intellectual curiosity
  • A note to your future Stanford roommate
  • What is meaningful to you and why
  • Additional short answers about your activities and life

Essay Writing Tips:

  • Share specific, vivid stories that reveal your character and perspective
  • Be authentic—admissions officers can spot manufactured narratives
  • Highlight your core values and what drives you
  • Show growth and self-reflection—how have you evolved?
  • Demonstrate how you'll contribute to the Stanford community
  • Avoid clichés, generic statements, and what you think they want to hear

Stanford weighs essays extremely heavily: compelling, genuine essays can elevate your application, while generic or poorly executed essays can undermine otherwise strong credentials.

Additional Success Factors

Recommendation Letters

Stanford requires three letters of recommendation:

  • One from your school counselor
  • Two from teachers (preferably in core academic subjects)
  • One optional additional recommendation

Strong letters should:

  • Provide specific examples of your intellectual curiosity
  • Discuss your character, leadership, and impact in the classroom
  • Offer insights admissions officers can't get from other parts of your application

Choose recommenders who know you well and can speak authentically to your strengths and growth.

Restrictive Early Action (REA)

Stanford offers Restrictive Early Action with a November 1 deadline. While not binding (you can apply to other schools later), REA applicants historically have shown higher acceptance rates — though this may partly reflect self-selection of highly qualified candidates.

REA is a good choice if:

  • Stanford is genuinely your top-choice school
  • Your application is strongest by November (grades, test scores, activities are solid)
  • You want an admissions decision by mid-December

Understanding Extracurricular Tiers

Not all activities carry equal weight. Stanford evaluates extracurriculars on a tier system:

  • Tier 1: Exceptional, rare accomplishments (national/international recognition, major awards)
  • Tier 2: Significant leadership or state/regional-level recognition
  • Tier 3: Solid participation and school-level leadership
  • Tier 4: Common activities without significant distinction

Competitive applicants typically have one or two Tier 1-2 activities that demonstrate their "spike"—the area where they truly excel and stand out.

Stanford's Student Body Snapshot

Understanding Stanford's student demographics provides insight into the university's commitment to diversity.

Ethnic and Racial Composition:

  • Asian: ~33%
  • White: ~24%
  • Hispanic/Latino: ~15%
  • Black/African American: ~8%
  • International students: ~14%
  • Multiracial and other backgrounds: ~6%

Geographic and Educational Background:

  • Students represent all 50 U.S. states and 70+ countries worldwide
  • 56% graduated from public high schools
  • 28% from private schools

Frequently Asked Questions About Stanford Admissions

  • what does Stanford look for in applicants? Stanford uses a holistic admissions process evaluating academic excellence, intellectual curiosity, meaningful extracurricular impact, compelling essays, strong recommendations, and personal character. They seek students who will contribute to and benefit from Stanford's diverse community.
  • does Stanford consider demonstrated interest? No, Stanford does not track or consider demonstrated interest in admissions decisions.
  • what is Stanford's Restrictive Early Action program? REA is a non-binding early application option with a November 1 deadline. If admitted, you are not required to attend, but you cannot apply early to other private universities.
  • What majors is Stanford known for? Stanford excels across disciplines but is particularly renowned for Computer Science, Engineering, Business, Economics, Biology, Political Science, and interdisciplinary programs.
  • Can international students get into Stanford? Yes, international students comprise about 14% of each incoming class. International applicants follow the same application process and are evaluated by the same holistic standards as domestic applicants.
  • What is Stanford looking for in essays? Stanford seeks authentic, reflective essays that reveal your personality, values, intellectual curiosity, and how you'll contribute to campus. They want to understand your voice, perspective, and what makes you unique.

Final Thoughts: Your Path to Stanford

With acceptance rates around 3.6-3.9%, Stanford University stands among the most selective universities in the world. Almost every applicant brings stellar grades and impressive test scores—the real differentiators are your intellectual curiosity, meaningful impact, and authentic story.

By combining academic excellence, genuine intellectual passion, deep extracurricular involvement, and compelling personal essays, you'll position yourself as strongly as possible for Stanford admission.

Remember that admission to Stanford—or any highly selective university—is never guaranteed, no matter how qualified you are. Focus on becoming the best version of yourself, pursuing what genuinely excites you, and applying to a balanced list of schools where you can thrive.

Why Most College Essays Fail (And How Yours Won't)

Most college essays fail because they sound generic, not authentic. Admissions officers read thousands of applications yearly—yours needs to feel real to stand out. Forgettable essays list achievements or use clichés like "I'm passionate about helping others". Memorable ones reveal who you are through specific stories and honest reflection.

This guide shares practical steps to write an essay that makes admissions officers root for you.

And scroll down to the bottom to download my Free College Essay Guide and Checklist for 2025!

Start With You, Not the Prompt

The Identity-First Approach

Most students approach essay writing backward. They read the prompt, brainstorm "impressive" topics, and try to fit their lives into predetermined boxes. This creates essays that feel manufactured and generic. Instead, try this exercise:

Step 1: Identify Your Core Values

List 5-10 values you genuinely live by. These aren't values you think colleges want to hear—they're what actually drives your decisions.

Step 2: Pick One Experience

Choose a specific moment that shows a value and connects to the prompt. For example, if curiosity drives you, describe staying up late researching a topic that fascinated you.

Example: I valued fairness, so I reorganized our debate team's practices to give everyone a chance to shine, leading to our first regional win.

Build a Strong Story Arc

Strong essays show change, not just a moment. Pick a story that reveals how you evolved:

  • Growth: You saw something differently over time. Example: I thought debate was about winning arguments, but a loss taught me to prioritize teamwork, so I redesigned our practices.
  • Challenge: You faced a hurdle and responded. Example: After losing regionals, I analyzed winning teams' strategies and led our team to a championship.
  • Curiosity: You followed an interest deeper. Example: Coding a game led me to build a text-to-speech tool for my brother with dyslexia.

Key Tip: Show your "before and after" to highlight growth.

Use Specific Details, Not Generic Statements

Clichés make essays forgettable; details make them yours. Avoid vague phrases like "I love science." Instead, describe unique moments.

Forgettable Memorable
"I love helping others." "I stayed up until 3 a.m. translating insurance forms for my grandmother."
"I'm passionate about science." "My kitchen experiment set off the fire alarm but proved my hypothesis."

Key Tip: Use concrete images to make your story unforgettable.

Specificity Test: If a sentence could appear in another student's essay unchanged, rewrite it with details only you could write.

Why specificity matters:

  • Specific details reveal personality and voice
  • Vulnerability creates a genuine connection with readers
  • Concrete images help admissions officers see you as a real person, not just another application
  • Unique moments can't be plagiarized or replicated

Write With Reflection, Not Just Description

Insight matters more than the story. Weak essays describe events; strong ones explain what they meant.

Questions That Generate Reflection

As you write, constantly ask yourself:

  • What did this experience change about how I think, act, or see the world?
  • Why does this moment still matter to me now?
  • What did I learn about myself that I didn't know before?
  • How does this connect to the person I'm becoming?
  • What would I do differently if I faced this situation again?
  • What questions does this experience leave me with?

Example: Weak vs. Strong

  • Weak: "I volunteered at a food bank, packing boxes and organizing drives."
  • Strong: "At the food bank, I saw families choose canned corn over apples due to cost. Researching food deserts led me to connect our food bank with farmers' markets. I learned caring requires asking tough questions."

Show Where You're Headed

Hint at who you're becoming without a rigid plan. Show curiosity and how college fits your journey.

  • Good: "I'm fascinated by how consciousness works, so I want to explore neuroscience and philosophy in college."
  • Bad: "I'll major in biology, attend medical school, and become a neurosurgeon."

Focus on questions that drive you and perspectives you'll bring to campus.

Key Tip: Show curiosity, not a 10-year plan.

The Window Metaphor

Think of your college essay as a window. If it's foggy, generic, or closed off, admissions officers can't see who you are or imagine you on their campus. But when you write with clarity, specificity, and reflection, you're opening that window and inviting them to see the real you—past, present, and future.

Common College Essay Mistakes to Avoid

Steer clear of these traps:

  • Inauthentic Writing: Avoid big words or fake humility (don't say "ameliorate" when "improve" feels natural).
  • Trauma Dump: Focus on growth, not graphic struggles.
  • Savior Narrative: Don't center yourself as a hero in stories about helping others.
  • Generic Ending: End with specific insight, not "This made me who I am."

Key Tip: Write in your voice and answer the prompt.

Understanding Different College Essay Types

Not all college essays are the same. Here's what you need to know about the main types: Different essays have different goals:

  • Common App Personal Statement (650 words max): Show who you are beyond grades. Reflect deeply on one story.
  • UC Personal Insight Questions (350 words each, pick 4 of 8): Share multiple angles of your life. Be concise, avoid repetition.
  • Supplemental Essays (150-300 words): Show fit with a school's programs or values. Research specific opportunities.

Key Tip: Tailor each essay to its purpose and word limit.

The Revision Process: How to Make Your Essay Great

First drafts aren't perfect. Follow these steps:

  • 1. Content: Ensure your essay shows growth, uses specific details, and answers the prompt.
  • 2. Voice: Read aloud to check it sounds like you. Cut unnatural words.
  • 3. Clarity: Shorten sentences, vary structure, and ensure smooth transitions.
  • 4. Proofread: Check grammar and typos after a 24-hour break.

Get feedback from 1-2 trusted sources (e.g., teachers, counselors), but keep your voice.

Key Tip: Revise multiple times to refine your story and voice.

Getting Feedback

Good sources:

  • English teachers who know your voice
  • College counselors with admissions experience
  • Trusted mentors who can give an honest critique
  • Parents (for fact-checking, not rewriting)

Best practices:

  • Ask specific questions: "Does this show who I am?" not "Is this good?"
  • Limit yourself to 2-3 trusted reviewers
  • Maintain your authentic voice throughout revisions
  • Know when to stop—perfection doesn't exist

Frequently Asked Questions About College Essays

  • 1. How long should my essay be? Use the full word count (e.g., 600-650 for Common App) but don't go over.
  • 2. What should I write about? A moment that reveals your values or growth. Mundane topics work if reflective.
  • 3. Can I use humor? Yes, if it's natural, but don't let it overshadow your message.
  • 4. Should I write about trauma? Only if you focus on resilience and growth, not graphic details.
  • 5. How do I start? Begin with a vivid moment or question to hook the reader.
  • 6. What makes an essay stand out? Authenticity, specificity, and reflection that feel like a real conversation.

What should I avoid in college essays?

  • Generic clichés and overused phrases
  • Trying to sound like someone you're not
  • Controversial political or religious arguments
  • Inappropriate or illegal activities
  • Negative comments about other schools
  • Quotes from famous people (use your own words)
  • Excuses for poor grades without context
  • Entire life story instead of a focused narrative

Final Takeaway: Your Story Is the Strategy

The "perfect" college essay doesn't come from sounding impressive—it comes from sounding like you. Your voice, your values, your growth, and your honesty are what admissions officers remember long after they've finished reading your application. They're not looking for students who've climbed Mount Everest or cured diseases (though those are fine topics if genuine). They're looking for thoughtful, self-aware people who will contribute meaningfully to their campus community. Think less about being extraordinary. Think more about being specific, reflective, and real. The essays that get students accepted aren't the ones with the most impressive achievements or the most dramatic stories. They're the ones where a real human being comes through on the page. That person is you. Now go write about it! Want more help? Follow @AvenirAdmissions on Instagram for weekly tips and essay examples.

1. Introduction

The University of California system is a top-tier public university network, attracting ambitious students worldwide. If you're aiming for Fall 2025 admission, mastering the UC application process is key to standing out. This guide covers test-blind policies, GPA calculations, course rigor, Personal Insight Questions (PIQs), and a step-by-step action plan to craft a compelling application for UC Berkeley, UCLA, or any of the nine campuses.

2. The Truth About Test-Blind Admissions

All UC campuses are fully test-blind for Fall 2025. SAT and ACT scores are not considered for admissions decisions, even if submitted—admissions officers won't see them. However, don't dismiss standardized tests entirely. Scores can still help with course placement after admission or qualify you for scholarships. If you've taken these tests, they're not wasted effort—just not a factor in getting accepted.

3. Understanding Your GPA: Weighted vs. Unweighted

The UCs calculate GPA uniquely, and knowing the difference is crucial:

  • Unweighted GPA: Your standard average across all courses, ignoring difficulty.
  • Weighted GPA: Adds extra points for honors, Advanced Placement (AP), International Baccalaureate (IB), or dual-enrollment courses. However, UC caps extra points at 8 semesters of advanced coursework to level the playing field for students from schools with fewer AP/IB options.

Pro tip: A slightly lower GPA with tough courses often trumps perfect grades in easier ones. Use the UC GPA Calculator to check your standing.

4. Why Course Rigor Matters

Beyond GPA, UC admissions officers prioritize course rigor. Taking AP, IB, honors, or college-level classes signals you're ready for UC's challenging environment. A B in AP Calculus can outweigh an A in a standard math class because it shows you're pushing your limits. If your school lacks advanced courses, highlight any available challenges (e.g., online courses or community college classes) in your application to demonstrate initiative.

5. UC PIQ Prompts 2025: Your Chance to Shine

The Personal Insight Questions (PIQs) are the heart of your UC application. Since test scores are out and holistic review is in, these essays let you showcase your personality, values, and potential. You'll choose 4 out of 8 prompts, with each response capped at 350 words.

Sample Prompt:

"Describe an example of your leadership experience in which you have positively influenced others, helped resolve disputes, or contributed to group efforts over time."

Tip: Focus on a specific moment—e.g., leading a club project that boosted school spirit—and reflect on what it taught you about collaboration.

Your PIQs should highlight:

  • Leadership: Show how you've inspired or guided others.
  • Creativity: Share unique ways you solve problems.
  • Resilience: Reflect on overcoming setbacks.
  • Impact: Detail contributions to your school, community, or family.

Strong essays provide context for your achievements and make your application memorable.

6. Your Action Plan for UC Applications

Verify GPA and A-G Requirements

Ensure you meet the UC's A-G course requirements and calculate your UC GPA to confirm eligibility.

A-G Course Requirements Overview

Category Years Required Examples
A: History/Social Science 2 US History, World History
B: English 4 Literature, Composition
C: Mathematics 3 (or 4) Algebra, Calculus, Statistics
D: Laboratory Science 2 (or 4) Biology, Physics
E: Language Other Than English 2 (or 4) Spanish, Mandarin
F: Visual/Performing Arts 1 Theater, Music
G: College-Prep Elective 1 Economics, Computer Science

Draft PIQs Early

Start brainstorming now. Write multiple drafts to refine your story. Aim for authenticity—admissions officers want to hear your voice, not a polished template.

Choose Your UC Campuses

Research campuses like UC San Diego or UC Davis to find the best fit for your goals. Each has unique strengths—e.g., UCLA for film, UC Berkeley for engineering.

Submit by December 1, 2025

The UC application deadline is December 1, 2025, at 11:59 p.m. PST (extended due to Thanksgiving). Submit early to avoid technical glitches.

7. FAQs About UC Admissions 2025

What if my school doesn't offer AP classes?

UC considers your school's offerings. Take the hardest courses available (e.g., honors or community college classes) and explain your context in the "Additional Comments" section.

How do I choose the right PIQ prompts?

Pick prompts that let you tell unique stories. For example, use the leadership prompt for a team project or the creativity prompt for a science fair invention. Read all 8 prompts on the UC Admissions website.

What's the difference between UC Berkeley and UCLA applications?

All UCs share one application, but campus selectivity varies. Berkeley and UCLA are the most competitive, so tailor your PIQs to reflect their values (e.g., Berkeley's activism, UCLA's innovation).

8. Final Thoughts

Applying to the UC system is about strategy and authenticity. Challenge yourself with rigorous courses, craft PIQs that reveal your unique story, and meet all deadlines. The UCs seek diverse, curious students who'll thrive in their communities—not just those with perfect stats. Your application is your story. Make it count.

Harvard’s acceptance rate for the Class of 2029 was 3.59%. Roughly 3–4 out of every 100 applicants are admitted. These odds are brutal, but the game is no longer exactly what it was five years ago. Legacy preferences are gone, donor influence is heavily curtailed, and—most importantly—the essay prompts and evaluation criteria shifted dramatically after the 2024 Supreme Court decision ending race-conscious admissions.

This guide reflects what actually moves the needle in the current cycle.

Introduction: What Changed and What Didn't

Harvard's acceptance rate for the Class of 2029 was 3.59%. Roughly three to four out of every 100 applicants were admitted. However, the 2025-2026 admissions cycle has seen several structural changes that shape who gets admitted.

What Still Matters

  • Near-perfect grades in the hardest classes available
  • Demonstrated intellectual vitality
  • An authentic, personal voice
  • A coherent application narrative supported by depth, not breadth

What's Changed Since 2024

  • Legacy preferences have been eliminated.
  • Donor influence has been significantly reduced.
  • Five brand-new Harvard supplemental essays were released in March 2025.
  • There is a greater emphasis on distinctive excellence ("the spike") over well-roundedness.

Academic Excellence: Still Table Stakes

Harvard is test-optional, but now explicitly recommends submission if your scores are strong.

Middle 50% of Admitted Students (Class of 2029)

  • SAT: 1500-1580
  • ACT: 34-36
  • Unweighted GPA: 3.93-4.00

Many admitted students have one or two A-/B+ grades because their course loads include many rigorous or challenging courses.

2025 Rules of Thumb

  • Take the most rigorous courses offered at your school and pursue opportunities beyond them, such as dual enrollment.
  • A 3.95 with extreme rigor is stronger than a 4.00 without advanced coursework.
  • Context matters: it will not be held against you if your school has a limited course selection.

The New Harvard Supplemental Essays (2025-2026)

These five 200-word prompts replaced the old free-for-all. Most applicants treat them like mini-Common App essays, and that doesn't tend to go too well. Here’s what each is really asking and a proven hook that worked in the 2025 cycle (anonymized).

  1. Discuss how your life experiences have shaped your perspective. This is the new “diversity” essay. Race/ethnicity can be discussed, but only through lived experience, not identity labels. Winning example hook: “At 3:17 a.m. on a Tuesday, my father, a night-shift janitor at the local hospital, texted me a photo of an empty PPE bin labeled ‘Property of Harvard Medical School.’ That moment crystallized the gap between the research I read and the reality my family lived.”
  2. Briefly describe an intellectual experience that was particularly meaningful to you. They want genuine nerdiness, not another leadership story. Winning hook: “I spent six months failing to prove the Riemann Hypothesis in my bedroom until a janitor at a math conference asked why I cared. His question hurt more than the math did.”
  3. You may share a topic, idea, or concept you find so engaging that it makes you lose track of time... Focus on pure intellectual vitality; go deep, not broad.
  4. Harvard's residential house system... How have you brought people together? This prompt seeks evidence of community and empathy.
  5. What are you grateful for? This acts as a maturity check; avoid generic answers.

Crafting a Coherent Narrative and "Spike"

A "spike" is a clearly defined area of excellence where you outperform 99% of peers and demonstrate measurable real-world impact.

A Spike is Characterized by:

  • Depth (multi-year commitment)
  • Impact (outcomes, not titles)
  • Originality (you do work that is not cookie-cutter)
  • Trajectory (you're still rising)

Weak Applications (far too common)

  • 12–15 unrelated activities
  • President of many clubs, mastery of none
  • Essays that contradict the activities list

Strong Applications (What Gets in Now)

  • 1-2 distinctive areas of excellence (e.g., research, arts, entrepreneurship, activism, STEM, humanities)
  • 2-4 supporting activities reinforcing the same narrative
  • Evidence of initiative and independent work

Activities That Stand Out in 2025

  • Original research published or presented at selective conferences or competitions
  • Building a tool, product, app, or startup used outside your school
  • Multi-year community programs with quantifiable reach
  • State/national recognition in creative arts, writing, or performance
  • Recruited varsity athletics (still meaningful, though less dominant than pre-2020)

Recommendations, Interviews, and International Applicants

Teacher Recommendations

  • Choose junior-year teachers who observed you at your intellectual peak.
  • One outstanding letter beats two average ones.
  • Letters should provide stories, not adjectives.

Interviews

Harvard interviews are now mostly non-evaluative. They should be treated as conversations, not assessments.

Strong interviews reflect:

  • Curiosity
  • Thoughtfulness
  • Comfort discussing your intellectual interests
  • Genuine personality

International Applicants

Harvard evaluates international students within the context of their country and curriculum. Strengths include national exams (A-Levels, IB, CBSE, WAEC, ENEM) and Olympiad-level achievement. Harvard does not expect APs or SATs if unavailable, but expects excellence in your local system.

Why Columbia (150 words)

Prompt: What attracts you uniquely to Columbia?

What works: Specifics like Core classes (Literature Humanities, Contemporary Civilization), NYC access, professors, and programs.

What doesn't work: Generic prestige language.

What works: Vision of yourself debating in Lit Hum or interning at specific companies in NYC.

Crafting a Coherent Narrative and "Spike"

Columbia seeks a "spike": distinctive excellence in 1-2 areas with real impact, aligned with Columbia's Core-driven intellectual community.

A Spike is Characterized by:

  • Depth (multi-year, independent pursuit)
  • Impact (tangible outcomes)
  • Originality (not resume-padding)
  • Trajectory (ongoing growth)

Weak Applications (too common)

  • Laundry list of 10+ unrelated activities
  • Titles without substance
  • Essays disconnected from activities

Strong Applications (What Gets in Now)

  • 1-2 deep spikes (e.g., research, writing, entrepreneurship, arts, activism)
  • Supporting activities reinforcing the theme
  • Evidence of self-directed learning fitting the Core

Spikes Don't Always Mean National Awards

Not every admitted student has published research or won international competitions. Here are examples of "quieter" spikes that demonstrate genuine depth:

  • A student who spent three years building a local tutoring program that became a district-wide model, training 50+ peer tutors
  • A poet who self-published a chapbook, ran community poetry workshops, and placed in regional competitions
  • A coder who built an accessibility app used by 200+ students at their school and presented findings at a local tech conference

The key is sustained commitment and measurable impact, not prestige.

Recommendations, Interviews, and the Rest

Teacher Recommendations

  • Choose junior-year teachers who observed you at your intellectual peak.
  • One outstanding letter beats two average ones.
  • Letters should provide stories, not adjectives.

Interviews

Alumni interviews are evaluative but conversational. Shine with: Curiosity about Columbia, thoughtful questions, passion for ideas.

Activities That Actually Stand Out in 2025

  • Independent research published/presented (Regeneron, conferences)
  • Building apps/tools/NGOs with users/impact beyond school
  • Sustained community initiatives with measurable change
  • National/international awards in arts, writing, debate, or Olympiads
  • Recruited for athletics or niche passions with elite achievement

International Applicants: What You Need to Know

Columbia conducts contextual review by country and curriculum—admissions officers understand the differences between A-Levels, IB, Indian CBSE, Chinese Gaokao, and other systems.

What Strengthens International Applications:

  • National exam performance: Excellence in IB, A-Levels, Baccalaureate, or equivalent demonstrates academic rigor
  • Olympiads and competitions: IMO, IPhO, national science fairs, debate championships
  • English proficiency: Demonstrated through essays, interviews, and optionally TOEFL/Duolingo (required for non-native speakers from non-English-medium schools)
  • Context-appropriate activities: Leadership and impact within your local community/school system

Key Points:

  • No SAT/AP expectation if unavailable in your region.
  • Columbia understands limited extracurricular infrastructure—focus on what you created or pursued independently.
  • Financial aid is need-aware for international students (more competitive), but full demonstrated need is met if admitted.

Final Thoughts + Checklist

Columbia seeks thinkers who thrive in the Core's shared intellectual adventure amid NYC's energy. Build depth, reflect authentically, and show how you'll contribute. These strategies have worked for thousands of students in recent cycles—they can work for you too.

Quick Checklist

  • Rigorous courses + strong grades
  • Coherent spike with impact
  • Intellectual curiosity in list/essays
  • Specific Columbia fit
  • Polished, reflective writing

Related Resources

  • Columbia Undergraduate Admissions

  • College Board

Cornell’s overall acceptance rate for the Class of 2029 hovered around 7–8%, but that number hides the most important truth about Cornell admissions: Cornell isn’t one school. It’s seven.

Each undergraduate college has its own priorities, faculty reviewers, academic expectations, and definition of excellence. There is no single “Cornell profile.”

This guide reflects what actually moves the needle in the current cycle, based on how Cornell evaluates applicants today, not how people assume Ivies work

Know the Cornell Philosophy

Cornell admissions makes more sense once you understand this core truth: Cornell prioritizes academic and mission fit over general prestige. Unlike many Ivies, Cornell:

  • Has no single numerical admissions index
  • Involves faculty directly in application review
  • Evaluates applicants within the undergraduate college they apply to
  • Includes New York State contract colleges
  • Places enormous weight on school-specific academic alignment

Your application is not judged against "Cornell applicants." It is judged against other applicants to your specific college. This is why strategy matters more here than almost anywhere else.

What Changed and What Didn't

What Still Matters

  • Exceptional grades in the most rigorous coursework available
  • Clear intellectual direction tied to a specific Cornell college
  • Evidence of independent curiosity beyond the classroom
  • A coherent narrative showing depth, not breadth
  • Authentic voice and purpose

What's Changed Since 2024

  • Continued test-optional policies across colleges
  • Increased emphasis on lived experience over labels
  • Stronger scrutiny of why you chose your college
  • Greater weight on faculty fit and academic intent
  • Essays that probe contribution, not consumption

Academic Excellence: Still Table Stakes

Cornell is test-optional, and applicants are not penalized for withholding scores. That said, academic readiness is a must.

Typical Admitted Academic Ranges (Contextual)

  • SAT (if submitted): ~1480-1560
  • ACT (if submitted): ~33-36
  • Unweighted GPA: typically 3.9+, reviewed in context

2025 Rules of Thumb

  • Take the hardest courses available to you
  • Rigor matters more than perfection
  • A slightly lower GPA with extreme rigor often beats a perfect GPA without challenge
  • Limited course offerings will not hurt you
  • International applicants are evaluated heavily on national/system exams

The Cornell Two-Rating System

Every applicant is evaluated in two major areas:

1. Academic Rating: How prepared are you to succeed in that specific college? This includes coursework relevance, academic trajectory, preparation for the major/field, and fit with the college's curriculum.

2. Personal Rating: How distinctive is your impact, leadership, and intellectual drive? Strong admits usually show strength in both, not perfection in one.

College Selectivity: Why Your Choice Matters

Selectivity at Cornell varies meaningfully by undergraduate college.

Most Selective (Overall)

  • Economics & Management (within CALS)
  • College of Arts & Sciences
  • College of Engineering
  • College of Architecture, Art & Planning

Still Selective, but Comparatively Less So

  • College of Agriculture & Life Sciences (CALS)
  • College of Human Ecology
  • School of Industrial & Labor Relations (ILR)
  • School of Hotel Administration

Cornell Supplemental Essays (2025-2026)

Cornell's supplements are school-specific and mission-driven. Strong Cornell essays demonstrate clear academic direction, reference specific faculty, research, or programs, show alignment with the college's mission, and emphasize contribution, not consumption.

Proven Strategy: Write as If You Already Belong. Strong essays answer:

  • How will you contribute academically?
  • What questions excite you?
  • What research or problems do you want to pursue?
  • What communities would you help shape or lead?
  • How do your interests extend beyond the classroom?

Crafting a Coherent Narrative & College-Specific "Spike"

A Cornell "spike" is not generic excellence. It is purpose-driven and depth aligned to one college.

A Strong Spike Shows

  • Multi-year commitment
  • Independent initiative
  • Tangible outcomes
  • Growth and trajectory
  • Clear relevance to the college applied to

Weak Applications (Too Common)

  • One resume for all colleges
  • Unrelated activities stitched together
  • Essays disconnected from coursework
  • Prestige chasing without direction

Strong Applications

  • 1-2 deep academic or impact areas
  • Supporting activities reinforcing that focus
  • Essays that sound inevitable for that college

Recommendations, Interviews, and the Rest

Teacher Recommendations: Choose teachers from rigorous junior/senior courses. Specific anecdotes are better than generic praise. One exceptional letter beats two average ones.

Interviews: Not all colleges offer interviews. When they do, they're evaluative but conversational. Curiosity, clarity of purpose, and intellectual engagement matter most.

International Applicants: What You Need to Know

Cornell conducts contextual review by country and curriculum. Strong international applications show excellence in national exams (IB, A-Levels, CBSE, Gaokao, etc.), depth within available opportunities, independent initiative where infrastructure is limited, and strong English proficiency through writing and interviews. Financial aid is need-aware for international students, but full demonstrated need is met if admitted.

Final Thoughts + Checklist

Cornell admissions isn't about being perfect. It's about being academically aligned, intellectually alive, and purpose-driven within a specific college. The right fit can change everything.

Quick Checklist

  • Rigorous, relevant coursework
  • Clear college-specific direction
  • Coherent spike with impact
  • Essays that show contribution
  • Polished, confident writing

UPenn’s overall acceptance rate for recent entering classes has hovered around 5–6%. But that number hides the most important truth about Penn admissions: Penn is not just “another Ivy.”

It is a mission-driven, pre-professional university where direction and execution matter deeply.

While Penn has fewer undergraduate colleges than Cornell, your school choice is still one of the most important strategic decisions in the process.

Know the Penn Philosophy

Penn admissions makes more sense once you understand this core truth: Penn prioritizes clarity of direction, real-world engagement, and academic-to-career alignment.

Unlike Ivies that emphasize open exploration, Penn:

  • Strongly values intentional academic direction
  • Emphasizes application of knowledge (research, internships, entrepreneurship, policy, healthcare)
  • Reviews applicants within the undergraduate school to which they apply
  • Encourages—but closely scrutinizes—interdisciplinary and dual-degree interest
  • Looks for students who will actively use Penn’s resources

  • Depth of involvement tied to future goals

  • Increased emphasis on why Penn specifically

Dartmouth's overall acceptance rate for recent entering classes has hovered around 6–7%. But that number hides the most important truth about Dartmouth admissions: Dartmouth is Unique in that it is a small, undergraduate-focused institution where fit, independence, and contribution matter more than polish.

This guide reflects what actually moves the needle today — and mirrors the seven strategies that separate strong applicants from admitted ones.

Know the Dartmouth Philosophy

Dartmouth isn't a mega research university.

It's a small, undergraduate-centered Ivy League institution built around close faculty access, deep relationships, and intellectual independence.

Fit matters here more than polish.

There is no single "Dartmouth profile."

But successful applicants consistently share key traits: curiosity, independence, and a willingness to shape both their education and their community.

Dartmouth looks for students who:

  • Thrive in discussion-based, intimate classroom environments
  • Build meaningful relationships with professors
  • Take ownership of their academic direction
  • Contribute actively to campus culture

Before applying, ask yourself:

Do I want mentorship over anonymity?

Do I enjoy small communities where impact is visible?

Am I comfortable designing my own path?

If the answer is yes, Dartmouth may be one of the best fits in the Ivy League.

What Makes Dartmouth Unique: The D-Plan

Dartmouth runs on the D-Plan, a quarter-based academic system that gives students an unusual amount of control over their time.

Students are required to be in residence for:

  • Freshman fall, winter, and spring
  • Sophomore summer
  • Senior fall, winter, and spring

From the remaining terms, students choose five additional residence terms, which may include:

  • On-campus study
  • Dartmouth-sponsored study abroad
  • Transfer or special academic programs
  • Internships or full-time work
  • Independent research
  • Travel and exploration
  • College-sponsored non-credit programs

This system allows students to pursue opportunities throughout the year — not just during summers.

Admissions officers are not simply evaluating whether you can handle a fast-paced quarter system.

They are evaluating:

  • Your ability to plan ahead
  • Your independence and maturity
  • How intentionally you design your education
  • Whether you understand how your academic interests fit the timing of your major

Strong applicants don't describe the D-Plan in general terms.

They outline specific plans for research, internships, global study, and academic sequencing.

At Dartmouth, how you use time is part of how you're evaluated.

Specialists > "Well-rounded"

Like many elite schools, Dartmouth values depth far more than breadth.

They are not searching for students who check every box.

They are searching for students with:

  • Clear intellectual focus
  • Sustained commitment
  • Evidence of growth
  • Impact beyond surface-level participation

At the highest academic and personal ratings, Dartmouth often sees:

  • Published research or advanced scholarship
  • National or international awards
  • Elite artistic or athletic distinction
  • Original inventions or entrepreneurial work
  • Early signs of future leadership in a specific field

You do not need national fame.

But your application should clearly show:

  • What you care about most
  • How long you pursued it
  • How deeply you've developed it
  • How it connects to your future direction

Dartmouth admits students who build expertise, not résumés.

Write Essays About What You'll Give Dartmouth

One of the most common Dartmouth mistakes is writing essays about how much you love the school.

Admissions officers already know what Dartmouth offers.

They want to know something far more important:

What will you contribute to Dartmouth?

Strong Dartmouth essays explain:

  • How you'll use the D-Plan to take academic risks
  • Which professors you want to work with and why
  • What classes or research pathways excite you
  • What clubs you'll join, lead, or create
  • How you'll shape both academic and social life

The most effective mindset is simple:

Act as if you already go there.

Strong applicants write as future members of the Dartmouth community, not as outside admirers.

Dartmouth rewards essays that show:

  • Intellectual independence
  • Initiative
  • Personality
  • A clear understanding of campus culture

Use Peer Recommendations

Dartmouth is one of the only Ivies that actively encourages a peer recommendation.

This is not symbolic.

It is designed to evaluate something that transcripts and test scores cannot: How you function inside a community.

The peer recommendation helps admissions officers see:

  • How you treat equals
  • How you lead without authority
  • How you handle stress and setbacks
  • How others experience you day to day

A strong peer recommender has seen you:

  • Lead teams or projects
  • Support others
  • Navigate conflict
  • Build trust
  • Create positive impact

This letter often becomes one of the clearest signals of:

  • Character
  • Leadership style
  • Social contribution

When done well, the peer recommendation can quietly strengthen competitive files and separate similar academic profiles.

How will you Shape Campus Life?

Dartmouth's small size makes its contribution highly visible.

On this campus, students are not anonymous.

Admissions officers look for students who:

  • Start clubs and initiatives
  • Take leadership roles early
  • Contribute meaningfully to traditions and community
  • Engage deeply in extracurricular life

Because leadership rotates term-by-term under the D-Plan, Dartmouth values students who:

  • Adapt quickly
  • Take ownership without waiting for titles
  • Commit intentionally by term

Strong applications highlight:

  • Initiative
  • Community-building
  • Leadership growth
  • A willingness to create, not just participate

Dartmouth admits students who don't just attend.

They admit students who help shape the institution.

Strategy Creates Real Leverage

At Dartmouth, selectivity is extreme — but strategy still matters.

Recent cycles show:

  • Overall admit rate: ~6–7%
  • Early Decision admit rate: ~20–25%
  • → A 3–4× admissions advantage

Early Decision sends a powerful signal:

  • Dartmouth is your clear #1
  • You understand the fit
  • You are ready to commit

Another meaningful signal of alignment:

  • Participation in Dartmouth Bound and other Dartmouth summer programs

These programs are not admissions guarantees.

But they are:

  • Strong indicators of interest and readiness
  • Especially meaningful for first-generation, low-income, and underrepresented students
  • Positive signals of cultural and academic fit

Real leverage comes from combining:

  • Strategic application timing
  • Deep Dartmouth-specific research
  • A focused narrative
  • Proven commitment through action

Fit + clarity + commitment move files forward.

Final Thoughts

Dartmouth admissions is not about perfection.

It is about being:

  • Independent
  • Intentional
  • Curious
  • Ready to contribute

The strongest applicants don't ask, "How do I get into Dartmouth?"

They answer a better question:

How will I use Dartmouth better than anyone else?
